sentences.text: Panoplosaurus is a genus of armoured dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.
Panoplosaurus mirus is the only known species of this extinct nodosaurid dinosaur, which lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America.
This quadrupedal animal measured roughly 5 meters in length and weighed approximately 1600 kilograms.
Its skull is broad and depressed, creating a triangular shape at the end of a blunt snout.
The skull measures 335 mm in straight-line length but spans 530 mm across the curved skull roof.
A prominent armour plate covering the cheek is present in the type specimen, though this may be a unique feature of the individual rather than the entire taxon.
Strong front legs with large muscle insertions suggest the animal was remarkably agile and capable of defensive charges similar to a modern rhinoceros.
First discovered in 1917, the animal was named in 1919 by Lawrence Lambe, with the name meaning "well-armoured lizard".
Charles M. Sternberg found the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — in 1917 in Quarry 69 of the Belly River Group, located 210 feet above sea level.

In 1981, a scapula from the Kirtland Formation in New Mexico was referred to Panoplosaurus, but it may instead belong to Nodocephalosaurus due to age and location differences, though this remains uncertain.
Specimens have also been reported from the Aguja Formation.
Microwear on the teeth indicates a diet of abundant foliage with occasional fruit.
The variability of the teeth implies a less restrictive feeding strategy than a simple soft-food diet.
Simulations suggest air passing through the nasal passages warmed by 17.9 to 18.2 degrees Celsius and became saturated with moisture.
The ground in its habitat was covered with mosses, lichens, fungi, and decaying plant matter.
The presence of gastroliths is uncertain because they were not found in the original specimen material.
Sternberg classified Panoplosaurus within the family Ankylosauridae in 1921.
He later described Edmontonia as a very close relative of Panoplosaurus in 1928.
Franz Nopcsa proposed a new classification for the genus in 1929 after describing Struthiosaurus.
Charles W. Gilmore amended Nopcsa's classification of Panoplosaurinae in 1930.
Panoplosaurus lived during the middle Campanian stage, roughly 76 to 75 million years ago.

Carpenter questioned the identification of four sacrals in Panoplosaurus in 1990, noting that Edmontonia has only three true sacrals, though he could not definitively identify the first sacral as a dorsosacral.
